author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Written in the mid-1970s and published posthumously in 1985, this novel splits PKD into two men—a Berkeley record-store clerk contacted by a satellite intelligence called VALIS and his skeptical writer friend—as they resist a fascist American president; it is the raw first draft of the 2-3-74 material later reworked into VALIS.
page_summary:
Set in an alternate United States ruled by the paranoid demagogue Ferris F. Fremont, the novel follows Nicholas Brady, a record-store clerk who begins receiving information in his dreams from an orbiting intelligence he comes to call VALIS. The transmissions heal his son, reorganize his life, and enlist him in an underground effort to expose and topple the regime by smuggling a subliminal message into a hit record. His friend Phil, a science-fiction writer, watches, doubts, and finally shares his fate when the security state closes in.

The book is PKD writing his own 1974 visionary experience straight into a plot: the benign satellite signal, the pink light, the Christian fish sign glimpsed on billboards, the sense of a hidden savior seeded into ordinary people. Empire and gnosis fuse here—the political tyranny of Fremont is the same occluding force PKD elsewhere calls the Black Iron Prison, and liberation comes as information breaking in from outside. What in later work he holds at ironic arm's length, here he narrates almost as testimony.

Rejected by his publisher in the 1970s, the manuscript was reworked into the 1981 novel VALIS and issued on its own only after PKD's death, in 1985. It reads as the fossil record of that transformation: the theophany as adventure story, before he split himself into narrator and madman to hold the material at a distance.

biography_events.event: PKD signs a Bantam contract for VALISYSTEM A (the alien-satellite plot, working title for what becomes RADIO FREE ALBEMUTH) with a December 1, 1976 manuscript deadline he describes as impossible to meet.
